videos.script: Lesson one ended with weights written by hand. This lesson finds them. {{loop}} A network learns by moving every weight a little against its gradient. The gradient says how much the loss changes when that one weight moves. {{nudge}} You could measure it by nudging each weight and running the network again. With twelve hundred and ten weights, that is two thousand four hundred and twenty runs for a single step. {{graph}} Backpropagation gets all of them from one pass forward and one pass back. It is the chain rule, applied from the loss towards the inputs. {{byhand}} You do it by hand first, on a network with nine numbers, and watch each gradient appear. {{tinynet}} Then the same rules become a small NumPy module called tinynet. Lessons four to eight build on it. {{check}} You check its gradients against the slow way, and see why that check needs double precision. {{train}} Then it trains for the first time, and gets more than ninety-five in a hundred validation digits right. {{vanish}} Last come ten layers of sigmoids. The gradient shrinks about forty-one thousand times before it reaches the first one. {{end}} That shrinking product is why deep networks were once so hard to train.
